claim: Protein production consumes an estimated 30-50% of the energy consumption of dividing cells.
source: Protein biosynthesis consumes a huge amount of energy: an estimated 30–50% of the energy consumption of dividing cells is dedicated to translation of the proteome (Buttgereit and Brand, 1995; Russell and Cook, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buttgereit and Brand, 1995 and Russell and Cook, 1995

claim: When the ratio of unneeded protein reaches 30% of total protein in bacteria, ribosomes are destructed and growth is completely inhibited.
source: As the ratio of unneeded protein reaches 30% of total protein in bacteria, ribosomes are destructed and growth is completely inhibited (Dong et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dong et al., 1995

claim: Protein burdens are most relevant shortly after an environmental change and are subsequently reduced once translation has adjusted to the novel steady-state level.
source: Protein burdens (i.e. protein overexpression costs) are most relevant shortly after an environmental change, and are subsequently reduced once the translation has adjusted to their novel steady-state level (Shachrai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shachrai et al., 2010

claim: Reduced viability was observed with the overexpression of proteins with no apparent cellular activities.
source: Gene expression costs are frequently not due to the detrimental activity of unnecessary proteins, as reduced viability was observed with the overexpression of proteins with no apparent cellular activities (Andrews and Hegeman, 1976; Dong et al., 1995; Kurland and Dong, 1996; Stoebel et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations: Andrews and Hegeman, 1976; Dong et al., 1995; Kurland and Dong, 1996; Stoebel et al., 2008; Scott et al., 2010

claim: Dosage sensitive genes in yeast are generally highly expressed.
source: Dosage sensitive genes were generally highly expressed, and replacement of the open reading frame of these genes with a green fluorescent protein (GFP) left the fitness cost largely unaltered.
evidence: Based on systematic study in baker's yeast by Makanae et al., 2013

claim: Replacement of the open reading frame of dosage sensitive genes with GFP left the fitness cost largely unaltered.
source: Dosage sensitive genes were generally highly expressed, and replacement of the open reading frame of these genes with a green fluorescent protein (GFP) left the fitness cost largely unaltered.
evidence: Based on systematic study in baker's yeast by Makanae et al., 2013

claim: Growth impairment results from the process of protein production and not from accumulating the unneeded protein product per se.
source: Studies in bacteria (Stoebel et al., 2008) and yeast (Kafri et al., 2016) demonstrated that growth impairment results from the process of protein production and not due to accumulating the unneeded protein product per se.
evidence: Supported by citations to studies in bacteria (Stoebel et al., 2008) and yeast (Kafri et al., 2016)

claim: Transcription dominates protein burden in low phosphate conditions.
source: Transcription dominates protein burden in low phosphate, while translation dominates costs in low nitrogen conditions.
evidence: Based on study by Kafri et al., 2016 showing that limiting factors vary across environments

claim: Translation dominates protein burden costs in low nitrogen conditions.
source: Transcription dominates protein burden in low phosphate, while translation dominates costs in low nitrogen conditions.
evidence: Based on study by Kafri et al., 2016 showing that limiting factors vary across environments

claim: The role of chaperone networks in contributing to protein burden has remained unexplored.
source: Yet, the role of chaperone networks in contributing to protein burden has remained unexplored.
evidence: Statement about gap in knowledge prior to this study

claim: Accumulation of an unneeded protein in yeast has a relatively mild impact on fitness when nutrients are in excess and no internal or external stresses are present.
source: In this work, we show that accumulation of an unneeded protein in yeast (S. cerevisiae) has a relatively mild impact on fitness when nutrients are in excess and no internal or external stresses are present.
evidence: Main finding from the study presented in the manuscript

claim: Impairment of specific molecular chaperones rendered yeast cells sensitive to gratuitous protein overproduction.
source: However, impairment of specific molecular chaperones rendered yeast cells sensitive to gratuitous protein overproduction.
evidence: Main finding from the study presented in the manuscript

claim: yEVenus expressed from a single copy plasmid has no detectable fitness cost.
source: From a single copy plasmid, yEVenus has no detectable fitness cost (t-test, p=not significant), while it confers around 2.5% fitness disadvantage from a high-copy plasmid (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from fitness measurements shown in Figure 1A with statistical testing

claim: yEVenus expressed from a high-copy plasmid confers around 2.5% fitness disadvantage.
source: From a single copy plasmid, yEVenus has no detectable fitness cost (t-test, p=not significant), while it confers around 2.5% fitness disadvantage from a high-copy plasmid (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from fitness measurements shown in Figure 1A with statistical testing

claim: When expressed from a high-copy plasmid, yEVenus constitutes approximately 3.7% of the total cellular proteome.
source: On the basis of a densitometry analysis using the standard curve, the yEVenus (band at 27 kDa) constitutes 3.7% of the total cellular proteome when expressed from a high-copy plasmid (for further details, see Materials and methods).
evidence: Experimental data from PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1B with densitometry quantification

claim: The amino acid composition of yEVenus and the yeast proteome are highly similar to each other.
source: the amino acid composition of yEVenus and the yeast proteome are highly similar to each other (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.6477, p<0.01)
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis of amino acid composition

claim: yEVenus is codon optimized specifically for yeast studies.
source: the amino acid composition of yEVenus and the yeast proteome are highly similar to each other (Pearson's correlation, r = 0.6477, p<0.01) and it is codon optimized specifically for yeast studies.
evidence: Property of the yEVenus construct used in the study

claim: Toxicity of yEVenus due to misfolding is negligible.
source: Accordingly, toxicity of yEVenus due to misfolding is negligible.
evidence: Inference based on the properties of yEVenus (rapidly folding, non-toxic YFP variant)

claim: At an ε = -0.05 cutoff value, 184 genes showed negative interactions with yEVenus.
source: At an ε = - 0.05 cutoff value (and using a p<0.05 cutoff based on bootstrap analysis), 184 genes showed such interactions with yEVenus.
evidence: Results from genome-wide genetic interaction screen

claim: Genes showing negative interactions with yEVenus overexpression are preferentially involved in translation, transcriptional control, mitochondria-related processes, and protein folding.
source: A functional enrichment analysis revealed that these genes are preferentially involved in translation, transcriptional control (e.g. transcription termination and elongation), mitochondria-related processes, and protein folding (Table 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Functional enrichment analysis of genetic interaction screen results shown in Table 1

claim: Deletion of genes encoding specific chaperones caused a 2-4 fold increment in the fitness costs of yEVenus overexpression.
source: Remarkably, deletion of genes encoding specific chaperones caused a 2–4 fold increment in the fitness costs of yEVenus overexpression (Figure 1E).
evidence: Experimental data from genetic interaction measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: Deletion of RPI1 removed protein burden.
source: Deletion of RPI1, a specific repressor of the Ras-cAMP pathway removed protein burden (Supplementary file 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Experimental data showing positive genetic interaction

claim: Partial inhibition of translation elongation by cycloheximide treatment elevated protein burden.
source: In agreement with expectation, partial inhibition of translation elongation by cycloheximide treatment elevated protein burden (Figure 2A).
evidence: Experimental data from chemical inhibition experiments shown in Figure 2A

claim: Treatment of cells with sub-inhibitory concentration (0.18 µg/ml) of cycloheximide leads to a 3.7-fold increase in protein burden.
source: Treatment of cells with sub-inhibitory concentration (0.18 µg/ml) of this chemical agent leads to a 3.7-fold increase in protein burden (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from cycloheximide treatment shown in Figure 2A with statistical testing

claim: Treatment of cells with sub-inhibitory concentration (30 µg/ml) of mycophenolic acid leads to a two-fold increase in protein burden.
source: Treatment of cells with sub-inhibitory concentration (30 µg/ml) of this chemical agent leads to a two-fold increase in protein burden (Mann Whitney U-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from mycophenolic acid treatment shown in Figure 2B with statistical testing

claim: Total depletion of non-essential amino acids from the growth medium resulted in a 2.5-fold increase in protein burden.
source: Total depletion of non-essential amino acids (0 arbitrary unit) from the growth medium resulted in a 2.5-fold increase in protein burden, compared to the regular one (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from amino acid depletion experiments shown in Figure 2C with statistical testing

claim: The relative fitness cost of yEVenus overexpression was not affected by the change of carbon source.
source: However, the relative fitness cost of yEVenus overexpression (left panel) was not affected by the change of carbon source. Specifically, the cost of yEVenus on glucose is comparable to that on galactose (t-test, p=0.14) or raffinose (t-test, p=0.07).
evidence: Experimental data from carbon source experiments shown in Figure 2D with statistical testing

claim: Growth media with alternative carbon sources (respirato-fermentative galactose, respirative raffinose) led to a reduction of absolute fitness by 27-32%.
source: Growth media with alternative carbon sources (respirato-fermentative galactose, respirative raffinose) led to a reduction of absolute fitness by 27–32% (right panel, t-test, p<0.001), compared to that on the standard carbon source (fermentative glucose).
evidence: Experimental data from carbon source experiments shown in Figure 2D with statistical testing

claim: The correlation between the fitness of the deletion strains and the strength of the genetic interaction was very weak.
source: Second, and more generally, the correlation between the fitness of the deletion strains and the strength of the genetic interaction was very weak (Figure 1F).
evidence: Statistical analysis of correlation shown in Figure 1F

claim: The list of genes showing negative interactions with yEVenus includes several members of the Hsp40-70-110 complex (FES1, SSE1 and YDJ1).
source: Most notably, the list includes several members of the Hsp40-70-110 complex (FES1, SSE1 and YDJ1), and an Hsp70-90 scaffold protein (STI1).
evidence: Results from genetic interaction screen

claim: The list of genes showing negative interactions with yEVenus includes an Hsp70-90 scaffold protein (STI1).
source: Most notably, the list includes several members of the Hsp40-70-110 complex (FES1, SSE1 and YDJ1), and an Hsp70-90 scaffold protein (STI1).
evidence: Results from genetic interaction screen

claim: Hsp70-associated proteins (FES1, SSE1, YDJ1, STI1) are functionally highly related.
source: These Hsp70-associated proteins are functionally highly related (Rizzolo et al., 2017), and all play critical roles in the ATPase activation and the nucleotide exchange regulation of the Hsp70 class Ssa chaperones.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzolo et al., 2017

claim: Hsp70-associated proteins (FES1, SSE1, YDJ1, STI1) all play critical roles in the ATPase activation and the nucleotide exchange regulation of the Hsp70 class Ssa chaperones.
source: These Hsp70-associated proteins are functionally highly related (Rizzolo et al., 2017), and all play critical roles in the ATPase activation and the nucleotide exchange regulation of the Hsp70 class Ssa chaperones.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rizzolo et al., 2017

claim: Impairment of Hsp70-associated proteins decreases the activity of Ssa chaperones and thereby perturbs the recognition and clearance of misfolded proteins.
source: Accordingly, impairment of these proteins decreases the activity of Ssa chaperones and thereby perturbs the recognition and clearance of misfolded proteins.
evidence: Inference based on known function of these proteins and citations to Mayer, 2013 and Clerico et al., 2015

claim: Aggregated proteins accumulate in the cell when Hsp70-associated proteins are impaired.
source: As a consequence, aggregated proteins accumulate in the cell (Mayer, 2013; Clerico et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayer, 2013 and Clerico et al., 2015

claim: Protein burden significantly increased with rising temperature, resulting in a 2.8-fold difference when colonies were subjected to 40°C compared to 30°C.
source: Protein burden significantly increased with rising temperature, resulting in a 2.8-fold difference when colonies were subjected to 40°C, in comparison to the optimal incubation temperature (30°C; t-test, p<0.001)
evidence: Experimental data from temperature stress experiments shown in Figure 3A with statistical testing

claim: Subjecting yeast cells to high temperature causes a severe proteotoxic stress as it induces protein misfolding of nascent proteins and perturbs proteome homeostasis.
source: Subjecting yeast cells to high temperature causes a severe proteotoxic stress as it induces protein misfolding of nascent proteins and perturbs proteome homeostasis (Trotter et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Trotter et al., 2002

claim: Incubation with sub-lethal dosage of AZC (2.5 mM) leads to a more than 4-fold increase in protein burden.
source: Incubation with sub-lethal dosage of AZC (2.5 mM) leads to a more than 4-fold increase in protein burden (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: Experimental data from AZC treatment shown in Figure 3B with statistical testing

claim: AZC is a toxic analog of proline, and incorporation of this chemical agent into proteins causes misfolding.
source: AZC is a toxic analog of proline, and incorporation of this chemical agent into proteins causes misfolding (Trotter et al., 2002; Albanèse et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Trotter et al., 2002 and Albanèse et al., 2006

claim: CTK2 and CTK3 are genes involved in controlling the fidelity of translation elongation.
source: Reassuringly, CTK2 and CTK3, two genes involved in controlling the fidelity of translation elongation (Röther and Strässer, 2007) were on the list of genes showing negative genetic interaction with yEVenus overexpression (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Röther and Strässer, 2007

claim: CTK2 and CTK3 were on the list of genes showing negative genetic interaction with yEVenus overexpression.
source: Reassuringly, CTK2 and CTK3, two genes involved in controlling the fidelity of translation elongation (Röther and Strässer, 2007) were on the list of genes showing negative genetic interaction with yEVenus overexpression (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Results from genetic interaction screen

claim: In wild type cells, protein misfolding propensity did not increase significantly upon protein burden.
source: In wild type cells, protein misfolding propensity did not increase significantly upon protein burden (Figure 3C).
evidence: Experimental data from protein aggregation assay shown in Figure 3C

claim: In genotypes impaired in protein folding (Δfes1, Δsse1, Δsti1, Δydj1, Δpfd1, Δgim5, Δcpr7), protein burden elevated the propensity of protein misfolding.
source: In these genotypes, protein burden elevated the propensity of protein misfolding (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Experimental data from protein aggregation assay shown in Figure 3C

claim: Aggregation frequency is 5-670% larger in the chaperone deletion mutants under protein burden, in comparison with the corresponding isogenic control strain with empty vector.
source: Aggregation frequency is 5–670% larger in the chaperone deletion mutants under protein burden, in comparison with the corresponding isogenic control strain with empty vector, respectively.
evidence: Experimental data from protein aggregation assay shown in Figure 3C

claim: 34 proteins were identified that bind to yEVenus after applying filtering steps.
source: After applying several filtering steps (see Materials and methods), we identified 34 proteins that bind to yEVenus (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Results from GFP co-immunoprecipitation assay

claim: The list of putative yEVenus interacting partners includes five proteins with chaperone-related functions.
source: Altogether, the list of putative interacting partners includes five proteins with chaperone-related functions (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Results from GFP co-immunoprecipitation assay

claim: Sti1p and Ydj1p bind to yEVenus and were also identified in the genetic interaction assay.
source: Notably, Sti1p and Ydj1p not only binds to yEVenus, but were identified also in the genetic interaction assay.
evidence: Results from both co-IP assay and genetic interaction screen

claim: Sti1p and Ydj1p are involved in the activation of Ssa proteins, key components of the Hsp70 complex.
source: Both proteins are involved in the activation of Ssa proteins, key components of the Hsp70 complex.
evidence: Known function of these proteins based on established scientific knowledge

claim: The co-IP method confirmed half of the 18 previously described Sti1p protein interactions under low protein burden.
source: Our method confirmed half of these 18 protein interactions under low protein burden, that is when yEVenus was expressed from a single-copy plasmid (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay shown in Figure 3D

claim: A significant drop in protein-binding affinity of Sti1p with 8 out of 9 detected interaction partners was observed under high protein burden.
source: Remarkably, we observed a significant drop in protein-binding affinity of Sti1p with as many as 8 out of the nine detected interaction partners under high protein burden (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay shown in Figure 3D

claim: Protein-binding affinity of Sti1p with Ssa1p decreased by 70% under high protein burden.
source: Most notably, protein-binding affinity decreased by 70%, 75% and 55% in the cases of Ssa1, Ssa2p and Hsp90p, respectively.
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay

claim: Protein-binding affinity of Sti1p with Ssa2p decreased by 75% under high protein burden.
source: Most notably, protein-binding affinity decreased by 70%, 75% and 55% in the cases of Ssa1, Ssa2p and Hsp90p, respectively.
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay

claim: Protein-binding affinity of Sti1p with Hsp90p decreased by 55% under high protein burden.
source: Most notably, protein-binding affinity decreased by 70%, 75% and 55% in the cases of Ssa1, Ssa2p and Hsp90p, respectively.
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay

claim: Protein-binding between yEVenus and Sti1p was detectable under high protein burden only.
source: Finally, protein-binding between yEVenus and Sti1p was detectable under high protein burden only (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Results from reciprocal co-IP assay

claim: Ssa1p, Ssa2p and Hsp90p are exceptionally important and well-characterized interaction partners of Sti1p.
source: This is all the more significant, as these proteins are exceptionally important and well-characterized interaction partners of Sti1p (Chen and Smith, 1998; Song and Masison, 2005; Balchin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Smith, 1998; Song and Masison, 2005; Balchin et al., 2016

claim: Deletion of genes involved in translation, transcriptional control, and mitochondria-related processes rendered yeast cells hypersensitive to protein overexpression.
source: First, deletion of genes involved in translation, transcriptional control, and mitochondria-related processes rendered yeast cells hypersensitive to protein overexpression.
evidence: Summary of main findings from genetic interaction screen

claim: Mutants with impaired mitochondria exhibit reduced respiratory growth and have to rely on less efficient modes of ATP production.
source: We note that mutants with impaired mitochondria exhibit reduced respiratory growth, and therefore they have to rely on less efficient modes of ATP production.
evidence: Inference based on known function of mitochondria

claim: Beyond ATP production, mitochondria are involved in the synthesis of certain amino acids.
source: However, beyond ATP production, mitochondria are involved in the synthesis of certain amino acids as well (Ahn and Metallo, 2015; Zong et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ahn and Metallo, 2015 and Zong et al., 2016

claim: The fractional contribution of yEVenus to the total proteome was not elevated in gene knock-out strains.
source: However, the fractional contribution of yEVenus to the total proteome was not elevated in gene knock-out strains (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Experimental data from fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 1D

claim: Allocation models that rely on transcription and translation only cannot fully account for protein burden.
source: This indicates that allocation models that rely on transcription and translation only cannot fully account for protein burden.
evidence: Inference based on the finding that yEVenus fraction was not elevated in knock-out strains

claim: The Hsp70 complex is a key player in the maintenance of normal proteostasis.
source: The Hsp70 complex is a key player in the maintenance of normal proteostasis.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about Hsp70 function

claim: Ssa proteins recognize and associate transiently with exposed hydrophobic patches of misfolded proteins in the cytosol and prevent protein aggregation.
source: The soluble Ssa proteins (members of the Hsp70 family) recognize and associate transiently with exposed hydrophobic patches of misfolded proteins in the cytosol and prevent protein aggregation (Mayer, 2013; Clerico et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayer, 2013 and Clerico et al., 2015

claim: Deletion of specific activators (YDJ1, STI1, FES1 or SSE1) of Ssa proteins substantially elevated protein burden and resulted in protein aggregation.
source: Deletion of specific activators (YDJ1, STI1, FES1 or SSE1) of Ssa proteins substantially elevated protein burden, and resulted in protein aggregation.
evidence: Results from genetic interaction screen and aggregation assays

claim: Ssa protein's capacity to bind and release client proteins heavily depends on activators YDJ1, STI1, FES1 and SSE1.
source: Indeed, Ssa protein's capacity to bind and release client proteins heavily depends on these activators (Wegele et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wegele et al., 2003

claim: The nucleotide exchange factors (Sse1p and Fes1p) are responsible for client-release and thereby support the refolding or the proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins.
source: In particular, the nucleotide exchange factors (Sse1p and Fes1p) are responsible for client-release and thereby support the refolding or the proteasomal degradation of misfolded proteins (Gowda et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gowda et al., 2013

claim: Due to partial functional redundancy of Ssa proteins, the corresponding SSA genes did not emerge in the screen.
source: It is worth noting that due to partial functional redundancy of Ssa proteins (Hasin et al., 2014), the corresponding SSA genes did not emerge in the screen.
evidence: Inference based on known functional redundancy (Hasin et al., 2014) explaining absence from screen results

claim: Temperature stress, elevated mistranslation rate and a chemical misfolding agent all substantially enhanced protein burden.
source: In agreement with expectation, temperature stress, elevated mistranslation rate and a chemical misfolding agent all substantially enhanced protein burden.
evidence: Summary of experimental results from stress experiments

claim: Molecular chaperones have an important role in buffering protein burden.
source: We conclude that molecular chaperones have an important role in buffering protein burden.
evidence: Main conclusion from the study based on multiple lines of evidence

claim: The distribution of genomic expression generally follows a highly skewed power-law like distribution with a small number of exceptionally highly expressed genes.
source: The distribution of genomic expression generally follows a highly skewed power-law like distribution with a small number of exceptionally highly expressed genes (Ueda et al., 2004; Lu and King, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ueda et al., 2004 and Lu and King, 2009

claim: Highly expressed genes contain various cost-minimizing gene architectures.
source: Highly expressed genes contain various cost-minimizing gene architectures (Frumkin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Frumkin et al., 2017

claim: Highly expressed genes are under especially severe selective constraints, possibly to avoid misfolding and consequent formation of protein aggregates.
source: Such genes are under especially severe selective constraints, possibly to avoid misfolding and consequent formation of protein aggregates (Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geiler-Samerotte et al., 2011

claim: yEVenus is a codon optimized fluorescent protein and is not particularly prone to misfolding and consequent toxicity.
source: It is important to emphasize that yEVenus is a codon optimized fluorescent protein (Sheff and Thorn, 2004), and is not particularly prone to misfolding and consequent toxicity (Kafri et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sheff and Thorn, 2004 and Kafri et al., 2016

claim: Several molecular chaperones can buffer the damaging effects of protein mutations.
source: More generally, several molecular chaperones can buffer the damaging effects of protein mutations (Csermely, 2001; Queitsch et al., 2002; Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Paaby and Rockman, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Csermely, 2001; Queitsch et al., 2002; Cowen and Lindquist, 2005; Paaby and Rockman, 2014

claim: Protein burden depends on genetic variation and environmental conditions.
source: In a similar vein, it appears that protein burden depends on genetic variation and environmental conditions as well.
evidence: Inference based on the study's findings showing variation across genetic backgrounds and environments

claim: The cellular capacity to tolerate major fluctuations in genomic expression heavily depends on the genetic makeup.
source: Therefore, the cellular capacity to tolerate major fluctuations in genomic expression heavily depends on the genetic makeup: the associated fitness costs should vary extensively across microbial species occupying different environmental niches.
evidence: Inference based on the study's findings about genetic and environmental variation

claim: Fitness costs associated with protein burden should vary extensively across microbial species occupying different environmental niches.
source: Therefore, the cellular capacity to tolerate major fluctuations in genomic expression heavily depends on the genetic makeup: the associated fitness costs should vary extensively across microbial species occupying different environmental niches.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the study's findings

claim: Promiscuous binding of Sti1p with certain globular proteins has no functional consequences unless the cellular dosage of the partner protein exceeds a critical threshold.
source: We speculate that promiscuous binding of Sti1p with certain globular proteins (such as yEVenus) has no functional consequences unless the cellular dosage of the partner protein exceeds a critical threshold.

claim: Protein burden promotes a partial disassociation of interaction partners from Sti1p, putatively leading to partial disassociation of the Hsp70-Hsp90 chaperone complex.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that protein burden promotes a partial disassociation of interaction partners from Sti1p, putatively leading to partial disassociation of the Hsp70-Hsp90 chaperone complex.

claim: Highly expressed proteins may indirectly influence protein aggregation in the cell by binding to key components of the chaperone network.
source: Specifically, our work raises the possibility that highly expressed proteins bind to key components of the chaperone network which otherwise would be used to navigate folding of other native proteins within the cell.

claim: Highly expressed proteins binding to chaperones may decrease the availability of active chaperone molecules, leading to increased propensity for damaging protein aggregation, especially in times of proteotoxic stress.
source: As a consequence, the availability of active chaperone molecules decreases, leading to increased propensity for damaging protein aggregation, especially in times of proteotoxic stress.

claim: Sti1p has an over 2-fold higher fraction of unstructured residues than the proteome average.
source: We hypothesize that Sti1p may be especially prone to promiscuous protein binding, as it has an over 2-fold higher fraction of unstructured residues than the proteome average (data not shown).

claim: Approximately half of Sti1p putative physical interacting partners are involved in the maintenance of normal proteostasis.
source: Approximately, half of Sti1p putative physical interacting partners (Cherry et al., 2012) are involved in the maintenance of normal proteostasis.

claim: The list of Sti1p interacting partners includes members of the Hsp70-Hsp90 complex, Hsp104 disaggregase, proteasome subunits and ubiquitin-associated proteins.
source: The list includes members of the Hsp70-Hsp90 complex, Hsp104 disaggregase, proteasome subunits and ubiquitin-associated proteins.

claim: Perturbation of Sti1p interactions by a highly abundant, weakly interacting protein would have serious fitness consequences in times of proteotoxic stress.
source: Therefore, one might expect that perturbation of Sti1p interactions by a highly abundant, weakly interacting protein (Figure 3D) would have serious fitness consequences in times of proteotoxic stress.

source: Cycloheximide binds the ribosome and inhibits eEF2 mediated translocation during translation (Obrig et al., 1971).

claim: Protein burden depends on the availability of amino acids in the environment.

claim: Genes with mitochondria-related functions, including mitochondrial translation, mitochondrial DNA replication and growth, and mitochondrial distribution and morphology are on the gene list identified by the SGA analysis.
source: Moreover, genes with mitochondria-related functions, including mitochondrial translation (e.g. MRPS9, MRPL22), mitochondrial DNA replication and growth (e.g. MMM1), mitochondrial distribution and morphology (e.g. MDM38) are on the gene list identified by the SGA analysis (Supplementary file 1).

source: First, the functional roles of genes that showed genetic interactions were far from being random (Table 1).

claim: Inactivation of genes involved in transcriptional elongation (HPR1, DST1, CDC73, ELP3) significantly increased protein burden.

claim: Mistranslation during protein synthesis promotes misfolding and protein aggregation.
